Project for Concept project

Grid composition studies

Feed design studies · 2025

No metrics. Concept work only.

Scope of work

  • Two nine-post grids composed as single surfaces
  • Alternating visual weight so no two heavy frames touch
  • A reading order that puts the strongest frame where the eye lands first
  • One palette held across nine frames without repeating a layout

Two self-set exercises in making nine separate posts read as one coherent grid. No client, no brief, no audience. The constraint was only the composition. There is no client, no live account, and no growth to report. The planning work is real; the numbers are not claimed.

Frames

What this is

Two grid exercises I set myself, with no client and no brief. The only constraint was composition: could nine posts, made one at a time, still read as a single deliberate surface when placed together.

Both are concept work. There is no account behind them and no results to report.

The problem with grids

Most feeds are built one post at a time, then judged as a whole. The seams show: two product shots land next to each other, or three text posts stack in a column, and the surface reads as a pile rather than a layout.

What I practised

  • Alternating weight. No more than two heavy frames touching, so the eye gets somewhere to rest.
  • Reading order. Placing the strongest frame where a new visitor’s eye lands first, not where it looked best in isolation.
  • Colour continuity. Keeping one palette across nine frames without every post looking the same.
  • Text budgets. Capping how many frames carry type, so the grid does not read as a noticeboard.

Herbal skincare, then eco technology

The first study works in earthy, botanical tones. The second pushes the opposite direction: a harder, more graphic palette where statement posts carry more of the load. Same composition rules, opposite mood, which is the point of running it twice.

What I would do differently

Plan the grid as a single canvas from the start. Designing nine posts and arranging them afterwards works, but the result is never as tight as deciding the layout before any frame is made. That is the habit I now apply to client work from day one.
